topic: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
parentTitle: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
title: Assessing and managing pain in children: FLACC, FACES and analgesic safety
blurb: Choose the right pain tool for a child's age and ability, score FLACC and FACES correctly, and apply the MHRA limits on codeine and aspirin.
question: Tom, 8, is going home after a tonsillectomy for obstructive sleep apnoea. His discharge prescription includes codeine linctus. What should the nurse do?

teach.h: Pain is what the child says it is
teach.body: Pain is an unpleasant sensory and emotional experience, and in children it is often under-recognised because they may not have the words, may hide it, or may show it through behaviour. The nurse's job is to choose a tool the child can use, score it consistently, act on the score and reassess. Plain English: ask the child if they can tell you; watch their behaviour if they cannot; and listen to parents, who know their child's usual signs.

teach.caption: Self-report is preferred whenever the child can give it. A behavioural tool fills the gap when they cannot.

letters.word: Legs: restless, tense, kicking or drawn up
Cry: moans, sobs, screams, frequent complaints
Consolability: hard to console or comfort

teach.caption: Each item scores 0, 1 or 2. Use the score alongside the clinical picture and your local analgesia plan, and always reassess after treatment.

teach.body: For babies, preverbal children and children with severe learning or communication disabilities, use a behavioural tool and ask parents or carers how their child usually shows pain. Changes such as stilling, unusual quietness or a particular sound may be that child's pain signal. Record the tool used and the score, give or escalate analgesia, add comfort and distraction, and reassess.

head: Situation
Rule
rows: Over 12 years, if paracetamol or ibuprofen fail
Lowest dose, up to 3 days, then review
teach.caption: Codeine is converted to morphine by CYP2D6. Ultra-rapid metabolisers can reach toxic morphine levels: drowsiness, pinpoint pupils, respiratory depression.

teach.text: Aspirin is not given to children under 16 unless a doctor or other healthcare professional prescribes it for a specific condition, for example Kawasaki disease. A parent who reaches for aspirin 'because that's what we used to use' needs clear advice to use paracetamol or ibuprofen instead.

teach.h: Scenario: Kai, 2, after a hernia repair
teach.body: Four hours after surgery, Kai is grimacing, kicking, arching his back, crying steadily and hard to comfort. Nurse Sam uses FLACC because Kai cannot self-report reliably, and scores Face 2, Legs 2, Activity 2, Cry 2 and Consolability 2: a total of 10. Sam gives the prescribed analgesia, asks Kai's mother to hold him, uses a favourite toy for distraction and reassesses after the drug has had time to work.

items: Ask the child first if they can self-report; use words they know.
Pick a tool for age and ability, and use the same one each time.
Involve parents, who know the child's usual cues.
Combine analgesia with comfort, play and distraction.
Reassess after every intervention and document the score.
Self-report is preferred; FACES from age 3.
FLACC: Face, Legs, Activity, Cry, Consolability; each 0–2, total 0–10; 2 months to 7 years.
Codeine: over 12 for acute moderate pain after paracetamol or ibuprofen; contraindicated under 18 after tonsillectomy or adenoidectomy for OSA.
Codeine is not used for cough and cold under 12.
No aspirin under 16 unless prescribed for a specific condition (for example Kawasaki disease).

summary: You can now pick a pain tool that fits the child, score FLACC and FACES correctly, and involve parents in reading their child's pain. You can also apply the MHRA restrictions on codeine and the aspirin rule for under-16s.

A.q: Tom, 8, is going home after a tonsillectomy for obstructive sleep apnoea. His discharge prescription includes codeine linctus. What should the nurse do?
options: Give it with a dose of paracetamol
Halve the dose and supply it
A.why: MHRA (2013): codeine is contraindicated in all under-18s having tonsillectomy or adenoidectomy for obstructive sleep apnoea, so the prescription must be challenged.

whyNot.0: Combining it with paracetamol does not remove the contraindication.
whyNot.2: A lower dose is still contraindicated; morphine toxicity is unpredictable.
whyNot.3: The 3-day limit applies to permitted use in 12 to 18-year-olds, not to this contraindicated use.

A.q: A student nurse asks how the FLACC pain scale is scored. Which description is correct?
A.why: FLACC scores Face, Legs, Activity, Cry and Consolability from 0 to 2 each, giving a total of 0 to 10.

whyNot.1: Each item scores 0 to 2, not 0 to 3.
whyNot.2: A row of faces chosen by the child describes the Wong-Baker FACES self-report scale.
whyNot.3: There are five items, not four: Consolability is the fifth.

A.q: Jamal, 4, has had an appendicectomy. He talks about how he feels and points to pictures. Which pain tool is most suitable?
A.why: Jamal can self-report and point. Wong-Baker FACES is a self-report scale for children aged 3 and over, and self-report is preferred.

whyNot.0: FLACC is for children who cannot self-report; Jamal can.
whyNot.1: A 0 to 10 number scale needs number skills beyond most 4-year-olds.
whyNot.3: Parents' views help, but the child's own report is preferred when he can give it.

B.q: Lucy, 11, has a sprained ankle. Her father asks whether he can give her aspirin at home. What advice should the nurse give?
options: Aspirin is fine at half the adult dose
Give aspirin with food to protect her stomach
B.why: Aspirin should not be given to children under 16 unless it is prescribed for a specific condition (for example Kawasaki disease). Paracetamol or ibuprofen are suitable.

whyNot.0: A smaller dose does not make aspirin suitable for an 11-year-old.
whyNot.2: Food does not change the under-16 restriction.

B.q: Kai, 2, is 4 hours after hernia repair. He is grimacing, kicking, arching, crying steadily and hard to console. What is his FLACC score?
B.why: Each of the five items is at its maximum of 2, so the total is 10.

whyNot.0: 5 would be a score of 1 for each item.
whyNot.1: 8 would mean only four items at the maximum.

B.q: Maya, 9, has severe cerebral palsy and does not use speech. After hip surgery, her mother says Maya goes very still and quiet when she is in pain. What should the nurse do?
options: Use a numerical scale with help
Score her pain using her mother's cue
Assume Maya is comfortable while still
Wait for crying before giving analgesia
B.why: Parents know how their child usually shows pain. Recording and using this cue with a behavioural tool gives a more accurate assessment.

whyNot.0: Maya cannot use a numerical scale even with help.
whyNot.2: Stillness is her pain cue, so assuming comfort would miss her pain.
whyNot.3: Crying may not be how Maya shows pain; waiting for it delays analgesia.

C.q: Ella, 14, has moderate pain after a fracture that has not settled with paracetamol and ibuprofen. Codeine is prescribed. What advice applies?
options: Lowest effective dose for up to 3 days
Combine it with codeine linctus at night
C.why: MHRA: in 12 to 18-year-olds use the lowest effective dose for the shortest time, limit treatment to 3 days and review if pain is not controlled.

whyNot.2: Doses must be at least 6 hours apart, within a daily maximum.
whyNot.3: Adding a second codeine product would exceed safe dosing.

C.q: Josh, 13, takes codeine for a dental abscess. He becomes very drowsy with pinpoint pupils and slow breathing. What does this suggest?
options: Normal sedation from good pain relief
C.why: Reduced consciousness, pinpoint pupils and respiratory depression are signs of morphine toxicity, seen in CYP2D6 ultra-rapid metabolisers.

whyNot.0: Allergy causes rash, swelling or wheeze, not pinpoint pupils with slow breathing.
whyNot.1: Under-dosing causes pain, not opioid toxicity signs.
whyNot.2: Pinpoint pupils and slowed breathing are not normal and need urgent action.

C.q: Ruby, 18 months, has returned from theatre after a forearm fracture repair. She is crying and drawing her legs up. Which approach is best?
options: Ask her to point to a face
Score FLACC and involve her parents
Wait until she can describe her pain
C.why: At 18 months she cannot self-report, so a behavioural tool such as FLACC (validated from 2 months to 7 years) is used, with parents' knowledge of her cues.

whyNot.0: FACES is for children aged 3 and over.
whyNot.2: A numerical scale needs number skills she does not have.
whyNot.3: Waiting leaves pain unassessed and untreated.

reteach.title: Can the child tell you?
reteach.question: What is the first question to ask yourself before choosing a pain tool?

blocks.body: If the child can tell you about their pain, use a self-report tool they understand: faces from about age 3. If they cannot, because they are too young, too unwell or have a communication disability, watch behaviour with FLACC and ask parents how this child shows pain. Then treat, comfort and reassess with the same tool.

blocks.text: A quiet, still child is not necessarily comfortable. Some children, especially those with disabilities, go still when in pain.

explain.body: Wong-Baker FACES is a self-report scale for people aged 3 and older. The child chooses the face that shows how they feel. Self-report is preferred whenever it is possible.

items.label: report: the child picks the face

test.q: From what age is the Wong-Baker FACES scale intended?
test.why: Wong-Baker FACES is for people aged 3 and older.

whyNot.0: Most 1-year-olds cannot point to a face to self-report.
whyNot.1: 2 months is the lower age for FLACC.
whyNot.3: 7 years is the upper age of the FLACC validation.

explain.body: Face, Legs, Activity, Cry, Consolability; each 0 to 2; total 0 to 10. Validated in children 2 months to 7 years after surgery (Merkel 1997).

test.q: A child is kicking with legs drawn up. What does the Legs item score?
test.why: Kicking or legs drawn up scores the maximum of 2 for Legs.

whyNot.2: No FLACC item scores more than 2.

explain.body: Codeine is for acute moderate pain only in children over 12 when paracetamol or ibuprofen have failed. It is contraindicated under 18 after tonsillectomy or adenoidectomy for OSA, and in known ultra-rapid metabolisers. Not for cough and cold under 12.

test.q: A GP prescribes a codeine cough linctus for Leo, 9. What should the nurse recognise?
options: It is suitable for children from age 6 years
Codeine is not used for cough under 12
It is safe to use for up to 3 days at most
test.why: MHRA (2015): codeine must not be used for cough and cold in children under 12.

whyNot.0: The cough and cold restriction applies to all under-12s.
whyNot.1: Weight-based dosing does not make it suitable.
whyNot.3: The 3-day course relates to pain in 12 to 18-year-olds.

explain.body: Children under 16 should not be given aspirin unless a healthcare professional prescribes it for a specific condition. Kawasaki disease is an example where aspirin is used under specialist care.

test.q: In which condition might a child under 16 be prescribed aspirin by a specialist?
test.why: Kawasaki disease is treated with IV immunoglobulin and aspirin under specialist care.

whyNot.1: Antipyretics do not prevent febrile convulsions and aspirin is not used.
whyNot.2: Migraine in under-16s is treated with paracetamol or ibuprofen, not aspirin.
whyNot.3: Paracetamol or ibuprofen are used for sprains.
